title: ArriveCAN App Procurement Controversy
description: A federal mobile application built during the pandemic whose budget ballooned from $80,000 to over $60 million. Auditor General audits highlighted conflicts of interest, missing documentation, and excessive consultant reliance.

timeline.event: ArriveCAN app launched for mandatory border health reporting.
Media reports disclose high outsourcing costs and subcontractor fees.
Auditor General releases report outlining a 'glaring disregard' for basic contracting procedures, noting the total cost was 'impossible to determine' due to poor record-keeping.
A company that worked on ArriveCAN is barred from federal contracts for seven years; a further Auditor General report finds contracts awarded to the firm did not follow the rules.
Federal Court rules against two senior public servants tied to ArriveCAN procurement in a challenge related to their cases.
A federal public servant is cleared of an allegation of improperly deleting ArriveCAN records.
RCMP investigation and parliamentary committee hearings on procurement misconduct.

latestDevelopments: The file is moving through the courts and internal administrative processes rather than through new audits, and coverage has been quiet since mid-2026. The most recent reported developments remain the April 2026 Federal Court ruling against two senior public servants connected to the procurement and the June 2026 decision clearing another federal employee over an alleged improper deletion of ArriveCAN records. A contractor tied to the app was barred from federal contracts for seven years in June 2025 after the Auditor General found its contracts breached the rules. No charges have been reported in the latest coverage, and the RCMP investigation has not produced publicly announced results.

title: Foreign Interference Public Inquiry
description: A national public inquiry led by Justice Marie-Josée Hogue examining allegations of foreign state actors (primarily China) interfering in the 2019 and 2021 Canadian federal elections.

timeline.event: Special Rapporteur appointed to investigate election interference allegations.
Hogue Commission formally established after opposition pressure.
Interim report confirms foreign interference took place but did not alter overall election outcomes.
Reporting notes that political party nomination and leadership races flagged as vulnerable by the inquiry have not led to rule changes in several parties.
Government moves to tighten federal election rules with measures aimed at foreign interference.
Government confirms the long-delayed foreign influence transparency registry will come into force in early August.
Registry takes effect; the foreign influence transparency commissioner states the new office alone will not prevent foreign interference.
Phase 2 hearings focus on policy recommendations and institutional defenses.

latestDevelopments: The file has shifted from inquiry hearings to implementation of the commission's recommendations. The foreign influence transparency registry came into force in early August 2026 after repeated delays, and the commissioner has publicly cautioned that the office by itself will not prevent foreign interference. Related legislation to tighten federal election rules was advanced in March 2026. No further hearings or new commissions have been announced since the registry launched, though commentators continue to argue that additional measures, such as platform rules and media literacy programs, are needed.

title: Sustainable Development Technology Canada Audits
description: Auditor General investigations found that the green tech funding agency approved over $330 million in projects that breached conflict-of-interest guidelines or funding eligibility rules.

timeline.event: Whistleblower reports raise concerns over conflict of interest in funding approvals.
Auditor General report outlines 96 instances of conflict-of-interest policy breaches.
Commons committee calls for a second, more in-depth audit of the agency.
Funding resumes under the National Research Council's IRAP program, with applications set to open in fiscal 2025-26.
Reporting describes the relaunched green technology funding program as significantly smaller than the former agency.
Board restructured, funding suspended, and oversight transferred to the National Research Council.

latestDevelopments: The controversy has wound down into a post-audit implementation phase and has gone quiet in national coverage. Funding restarted in 2025 through the National Research Council's IRAP program, and May 2026 reporting described the relaunched greentech program as a much smaller successor to the former agency. No new audit findings, charges or committee proceedings have been reported since, and the last known state is that oversight remains with the National Research Council.

title: Freedom Convoy 2022 Endorsements
description: Criticism and political backlash over prominent Conservative MPs publicly meeting with, supporting, and endorsing the leaders of the 2022 truck convoy protests that blockaded Ottawa.

timeline.event: Convoy blockades streets in downtown Ottawa.
Opposition MPs meet with protesters; Emergencies Act is invoked.
Public Order Emergency Commission rules invocation of the Act was justified, noting political polarization.
Federal Court of Appeal issues its decision in the litigation over the 2022 Emergencies Act invocation; the Canadian Civil Liberties Association describes the ruling as a victory.
Polling four years after the protest finds Canadians remain divided over the convoy.
Ongoing debate and legal appeals over the limits of protest and emergency powers.

latestDevelopments: The political controversy over MPs' endorsements is effectively settled, and recent coverage consists mainly of commentary rather than new developments. The underlying legal question was addressed by a January 2026 Federal Court of Appeal decision on the legality of the 2022 Emergencies Act invocation, which the Canadian Civil Liberties Association called a historic victory; a further appeal remains possible. Polling in March 2026 showed public opinion still divided four years on, and no parliamentary or regulatory process is currently under way.

title: Leadership Election Expense Audits
description: Elections Canada compliance reviews and internal party friction regarding leadership campaign spending limits, corporate donations, and expense declarations from recent leadership races.

timeline.event: CPC leadership vote concludes.
Elections Canada reviews campaign expenditure audits.
Ongoing debate and audit reconciliation processes.

latestDevelopments: There is no recent news specific to the leadership campaign expense audits, which appear to be handled administratively by Elections Canada, and the story has gone quiet. The most recent related coverage, in July 2026, dealt with the Conservative Party's routine annual financial returns, which showed roughly $85 million in revenue and a $14-million deficit for 2025, with election-year spending nearly double that of the Liberals. No regulator has announced findings of wrongdoing connected to the leadership races.

title: Supply and Confidence Agreement Backlash
description: Criticism from political opponents that the NDP's formal deal to prop up the Liberal minority government in exchange for dentalcare and pharmacare was an undemocratic coalition.

timeline.event: Liberals and NDP sign a formal Supply and Confidence Agreement.
Pharmacare framework passed, fulfilling a key NDP condition.
NDP leader terminates the formal agreement early, shifting to case-by-case votes.

latestDevelopments: This dispute is dormant. The agreement ended in September 2024 and the dental and pharmacare programs created under it remain in place. Recent headlines touching the topic are limited to commentary and an unverified report that the former NDP leader was being considered for a federal appointment, rather than any new process, investigation or inquiry. The political argument over the arrangement has faded from national coverage.

title: Old Age Security (OAS) Pension Leverage
description: Political debate over the Bloc Québécois leveraging their balance-of-power status in the minority parliament to demand the government pass Bill C-319 to increase seniors pensions, facing criticism over fiscal costs.

timeline.event: Bloc sets a deadline for the government to approve the pension hike.
Deadline passes without government compliance; confidence debates triggered.
Legislative negotiations on senior benefits continue.

latestDevelopments: The confrontation over Bill C-319 has gone quiet, with no recent headlines about Bloc ultimatums or confidence votes tied to seniors' benefits. Coverage through September 2026 is limited to routine reporting on OAS and CPP payment dates and indexed amounts, including a quarterly increase taking effect in October and maximum monthly OAS payments cited at up to roughly $827 depending on age bracket, alongside stories about seniors' cost-of-living pressures and debate over the retirement age. The last known state is that the Bloc's demanded across-the-board increase for seniors aged 65 to 74 was not enacted.

title: Alto Rail Project and Ministerial Conflict-of-Interest Questions
description: Opposition MPs have alleged potential conflicts of interest involving a cabinet minister's connections to the Alto high-speed rail project, and have raised questions about Prime Minister Mark Carney's prior private-sector ties. Nothing has been proven, and the matters have been pursued primarily through the House ethics committee and calls for an ethics commissioner investigation.

timeline.event: House ethics committee orders a study of the Conflict of Interest Act.
MPs vote to summon the Prime Minister's chief of staff, the Clerk of the Privy Council and Brookfield officials to testify; reporting notes scrutiny of Carney's former business ties.
Conservatives call for an investigation into a minister's connection to the Alto rail project; the Prime Minister defends the minister.
The ethics commissioner states there is 'no risk' of a potential conflict of interest arising from Minister Champagne's partner working for Alto.
Conservatives allege Minister Champagne is avoiding a committee study of the Alto rail connection.
A Conservative MP calls for an ethics probe into the finance minister over the Alto rail project.
Liberal members shut down debate at the House ethics committee on a proposed study into an alleged condominium 'bailout' linked to the Prime Minister.
Reports indicate Ontario is reconsidering its support for the federal Alto high-speed rail project after Ottawa rejected a Billy Bishop airport expansion.

latestDevelopments: The conflict-of-interest questions remain a parliamentary matter rather than a court or police file, and no finding of wrongdoing has been made; the ethics commissioner said in April 2026 that there was 'no risk' of a conflict from Minister Champagne's partner working for Alto, while opposition MPs continued to seek a committee study and a further probe. In July 2026 Liberal members shut down committee debate on a separate proposed study into an alleged condominium 'bailout' involving the Prime Minister. Since then, coverage has centred on the project itself — Ontario reconsidering its support after Ottawa rejected a Billy Bishop airport expansion, questions from eastern Ontario MPPs, a possible Kingston stop, local protests, and calls for greater federal transparency on the plan. No new ethics proceedings have been announced.
